chat.title: Long thread on SQLite journal modes

messages.content: Hi! Long session ahead — I'm migrating a desktop app's storage to SQLite and want to understand journal modes properly.
Happy to go deep. The short version: the default rollback journal mode blocks writers while readers hold the database; WAL mode lets readers and the writer proceed concurrently.
Before we dive in, what's the weather like where you are? Haha, kidding. Okay, why does WAL allow concurrent reads?

WAL appends changes to a write-ahead log instead of overwriting pages. Readers keep reading the main database file as of their snapshot; only a checkpoint copies committed pages back. So a writer appending to the log never disturbs an active reader.
What are the downsides then?

The WAL file can grow until a checkpoint runs, bulk imports are slower if they produce huge logs, and WAL needs shared-memory support on the filesystem — network filesystems are a common failure case.
Right, we had NFS issues with other databases before. How do checkpoints actually happen?

Automatically: when the WAL reaches 1000 pages by default, SQLite runs a passive checkpoint in the background of whatever connection committed. You can also PRAGMA wal_checkpoint manually, with TRUNCATE or RESTART to shrink the file.
Is a passive checkpoint allowed to fail?
Yes — it skips pages that readers are still using. That's fine; they'll be checkpointed later. The database stays consistent either way.
Switching topics for a second — do you know a good snack for long coding sessions?
Nuts and fruit keep the hands busy without the keyboard crumbs of chips. But back to SQLite whenever you're ready!
Haha okay. Now: what pragmas do you recommend alongside WAL for a desktop app?
Typically: journal_mode=WAL, synchronous=NORMAL (safe with WAL, much faster than FULL), a busy_timeout of a few seconds, and temp_store=MEMORY. Keep one writer connection and serialize writes.
Why does synchronous=NORMAL stay safe under WAL?

The WAL protocol only needs the log durable at checkpoint boundaries; NORMAL fsyncs at those points. A power loss can lose the last transaction but never corrupts the database — FULL additionally protects every commit at a large speed cost.
Got it. And busy_timeout — does it apply to lock acquisition only?
It bounds how long a connection retries when it finds the database locked, writer or reader. When it expires you get SQLITE_BUSY; in WAL you mostly see it between competing writers.
We'll have one writer anyway. What about memory-mapped I/O?
mmap_size can speed read-heavy workloads by mapping the file, but keep it modest and remember it adds no safety. For a desktop app with moderate data, default paging is usually enough.
Fair. How do I migrate an existing database file to WAL without losing data?
Just run PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL on the open database; it converts in place. Do it once and persist it — the journal mode is stored in the file header, so it survives restarts.
And back again if we ever need to?
Same pragma with DELETE. One caveat: you need exclusive access during the switch, and a checkpoint runs to fold the log back in.
What happens to the WAL and SHM files when the last connection closes?
A clean close checkpoints and deletes both files by default. If you see a leftover WAL, something exited uncleanly — the next open recovers it automatically.
Reassuring. One more: does WAL change how vacuum works?
VACUUM still rebuilds the database; under WAL it writes through the log like any other change. It briefly needs disk space for the copy, and you can't run it inside a transaction.
We rarely delete rows, so vacuum probably doesn't matter much. Anything else you'd warn about for desktop SQLite?

Three things: keep the database off synced network volumes, open with a single writer, and set a realistic busy_timeout. Also back up by copying with the online backup API rather than copying raw files mid-write.
The backup API — does that just hold a read transaction?
It iterates pages under a consistent snapshot, so it's safe while writers proceed (under WAL). sqlite3 .backup uses it under the hood.
Perfect. Last one for today: how do I verify all this is actually in effect after opening the database?
Query the pragmas back: journal_mode should answer 'wal', and synchronous should report 1 (NORMAL). Add a startup sanity check that fails fast if the file was created with different settings.
Great, that's everything for now. Thanks for the marathon session!
Anytime — good luck with the migration!
